BiomedXPro: Prompt Optimization for Explainable Diagnosis with Biomedical Vision Language Models

Kaushitha Silva ††thanks: Equal contribution Affiliation: University of Peradeniya Affiliation: Peradeniya, Sri Lanka Email: e19372@eng.pdn.ac.lk    Mansitha Eashwara11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of Peradeniya Affiliation: Peradeniya, Sri Lanka Email: e19094@eng.pdn.ac.lk    Sanduni Ubayasiri11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of Peradeniya Affiliation: Peradeniya, Sri Lanka Email: e19408@eng.pdn.ac.lk    Ruwan Tennakoon Affiliation: RMIT University Affiliation: Melbourne, Australia Email: ruwan.tennakoon@rmit.edu.au    Damayanthi Herath Affiliation: University of Peradeniya Affiliation: Peradeniya, Sri Lanka Email: damayanthiherath@eng.pdn.ac.lk
Abstract

The clinical adoption of biomedical vision-language models is hindered by prompt optimization techniques that produce either uninterpretable latent vectors or single textual prompts. This lack of transparency and failure to capture the multi-faceted nature of clinical diagnosis, which relies on integrating diverse observations, limits their trustworthiness in high-stakes settings. To address this, we introduce BiomedXPro, an evolutionary framework that leverages a large language model as both a biomedical knowledge extractor and an adaptive optimizer to automatically generate a diverse ensemble of interpretable, natural-language prompt pairs for disease diagnosis. Experiments on multiple biomedical benchmarks show that BiomedXPro consistently outperforms state-of-the-art prompt-tuning methods, particularly in data-scarce few-shot settings. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates a strong semantic alignment between the discovered prompts and statistically significant clinical features, grounding the model’s performance in verifiable concepts. By producing a diverse ensemble of interpretable prompts, BiomedXPro provides a verifiable basis for model predictions, representing a critical step toward the development of more trustworthy and clinically-aligned AI systems.

1 Introduction

Accurate and transparent interpretation of biomedical images is fundamental for reliable disease diagnosis. In clinical practice, radiologists, pathologists, and other medical specialists rely on well-established visual cues such as cellular morphology, tissue architecture, and pathological patterns, combined with domain expertise, to make informed diagnostic decisions. For computer vision systems to achieve clinical acceptance, they must not only demonstrate high predictive accuracy but also provide interpretable outputs that align with established clinical reasoning processes.

Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), particularly Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) [14], have demonstrated remarkable potential for bridging visual content with natural language descriptions. Biomedical adaptations such as BiomedCLIP [21] extend these capabilities to medical imaging domains. While CLIP models demonstrate strong zero-shot capabilities, their performance often benefits from prompt optimization tailored to specific tasks. Early attempts relied on manual prompt engineering [14], which was labor-intensive and required domain expertise. To overcome these challenges, gradient-based prompt learning methods such as Context Optimization (CoOp) [24] introduced learnable soft prompts represented as continuous vectors optimized via gradient descent. Biomedical adaptations, including BiomedCoOp [10] and XCoOp [1], incorporated domain knowledge into CoOp frameworks to improve performance.

Despite these advances, two critical challenges remain for clinical adoption: (1) prompts used to guide these models are typically optimized as uninterpretable feature vectors, providing no insight into the underlying diagnostic rationale [10, 1, 3], and (2) existing methods generally produce singular prompts, restricting their ability to capture the multifaceted nature of clinical observations that practitioners routinely consider.

Large Language Models (LLMs) present a compelling solution to these limitations. They can generate semantically meaningful, natural-language prompts that encode biomedical knowledge and can be automatically refined to enhance diagnostic performance [25, 20]. However, existing LLM-driven prompt optimization techniques still operate largely as black-box systems, with limited mechanisms to ensure clinical transparency or domain relevance.

In this work, we introduce BiomedXPro, an evolutionary prompting framework specifically designed for biomedical disease diagnosis. Unlike conventional methods that seek a single optimal prompt, our framework evolves a diverse ensemble of human-readable prompts, each capturing distinct diagnostic observations. These prompts may emphasize specific morphological alterations, tissue organizational patterns, or cellular-level abnormalities that are directly interpretable by clinical practitioners. We leverage LLMs both as biomedical knowledge extractors and as adaptive optimizers that iteratively refine prompts through structured feedback mechanisms, ensuring that the final prompt ensemble captures a comprehensive range of clinically meaningful features.

Our approach delivers three key advantages for clinical integration:

  1. 1.

    Interpretability: Each optimized prompt corresponds to a clear, medically grounded observation, providing transparency into model decision-making processes and enabling clinical validation.

  2. 2.

    Diversity: Maintaining multiple complementary prompts mirrors the multi-perspective approach that clinicians naturally employ when evaluating diagnostic evidence, enhancing model robustness and generalization capabilities.

  3. 3.

    Clinical Trustworthiness: Probabilistic predictions are anchored in semantically meaningful medical concepts, facilitating their integration into established diagnostic workflows and supporting evidence-based clinical decision-making.

By combining the adaptability of vision-language models with interpretable, LLM-driven prompt evolution, our framework goes beyond conventional accuracy-focused approaches and directly addresses the fundamental barriers to safe and trustworthy deployment of AI systems in clinical diagnostic environments.

2 Related work

2.1 VLMs in biomedical imaging

VLMs like CLIP [14] have revolutionized multi-modal learning by aligning images and text through contrastive pre-training, enabling strong zero-shot capabilities. However, their direct application to the biomedical domain is challenged by specialized terminology, subtle visual markers, and the scarcity of labeled data [22]. To overcome these limitations, domain-adapted models such as MedCLIP [18], PubMedCLIP [4], and BiomedCLIP [21] have been developed. These models, by incorporating biomedical-specific pretraining strategies, have demonstrated superior performance on biomedical tasks.

BiomedCLIP, trained on over 15 million biomedical image-text pairs with a PubMedBERT encoder, has notably established state-of-the-art results across multiple biomedical vision-language benchmarks. While it offers strong zero-shot performance, its effectiveness can be further enhanced by adapting it to specific tasks. This is where prompt tuning becomes critical, as it efficiently tailors a frozen VLM for a new task without full model fine-tuning. This method involves optimizing a text prompt or its token level representation to guide the model toward the most relevant information, thereby capturing the fine-grained, disease-specific nuances that are essential in clinical applications and enhancing performance even in low-data settings.

2.2 Limitations of soft prompt tuning

Soft prompt tuning methods, which learn textual tokens appended to natural-language prompts, offer lightweight alternatives to full model fine-tuning. Context Optimization (CoOp) [24] introduced learnable soft prompts optimized via gradient descent under a frozen CLIP backbone. However, soft prompts often remain uninterpretable and may overfit in low-shot settings, limiting their applicability in high-stakes biomedical contexts where explainability is paramount. While recent adaptations like BiomedCoOp [10] and XCoOp [1] incorporate LLM-generated knowledge to improve performance and guide the learning process, they still fundamentally rely on uninterpretable soft prompts. Despite their advancements, the final learned prompts in these methods lack the true human-readability necessary for transparent and trustworthy clinical applications.

2.3 Hard prompt tuning

While soft prompts offer efficiency, their lack of transparency limits their use in clinical settings. Hard prompt tuning, which optimizes explicit text strings, improves interpretability but relies heavily on manual design and domain expertise. To overcome this, recent methods leverage LLMs for automated prompt generation. Approaches such as APE [25] and OPRO [20] treat prompt design as a black-box optimization problem, while frameworks like EvoPrompt [7] and PromptBreeder [5] integrate evolutionary algorithms to iteratively refine prompts, achieving stronger generalization than manual engineering.

These techniques have been extended to VLMs, with works such as Liu et al. [11] and IPO [3] demonstrating that interpretable, LLM-generated prompts reduce overfitting and improve transferability compared to gradient-based CoOp. Evolutionary approaches like ProAPO [13] further improve efficiency by refining prompts through mutation and crossover while limiting repeated LLM queries.

Despite their promise, direct adaptation to biomedical imaging remains challenging. Many methods assume access to large general-domain corpora or rely on multimodal LLMs that struggle with biomedical specificity. Moreover, constraints such as limited initial prompt diversity (e.g., ProAPO) and incomplete integration of insights from broader prompt optimization research (e.g., handling recency bias, scoring formats) highlight open opportunities for advancing interpretable prompt tuning in BiomedCLIP and related models.

2.4 Explainability in biomedical CLIP models

Interpretability remains critical for clinical adoption. Extensions such as XCoOp [1] and BiomedCoOp [10] improve transparency by incorporating clinical knowledge extracted via LLMs, yet the learned soft prompts remain latent vectors with limited human readability.

An alternative is descriptor-based prompting, as in Xplainer [12], which classifies images based on structured radiological observations (e.g., “There is/are [no] [observation] indicating [pathology]”). This offers inherent interpretability, but its effectiveness depends on initial LLM-generated prompts and extensive manual engineering by domain experts, making it difficult to generalize across diverse biomedical tasks.

3 Methodology

3.1 Problem formulation

Given a biomedical dataset 𝒟={(xi,yi)}i=1N\mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} with medical images xi∈ℝH×W×Cx_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C} and binary labels yi∈{0,1},y_{i}\in\{0,1\}, we address the challenge of learning interpretable visual concepts for disease classification. We leverage a pre-trained VLM with an image encoder fθ:ℝH×W×C→ℝdf_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} and a text encoder gϕ:𝒯→ℝd,g_{\phi}:\mathcal{T}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}, which project visual and textual inputs into a shared dd-dimensional embedding space.

Our goal is to discover a set of KK semantically meaningful prompt pairs:

P={(pj−,pj+)}j=1K,pj−,pj+∈𝒯,P=\{(p_{j}^{-},p_{j}^{+})\}_{j=1}^{K},\quad p_{j}^{-},p_{j}^{+}\in\mathcal{T}, (1)

where pj+p_{j}^{+} describes the presence of disease-indicative visual observations and pj−p_{j}^{-} describes their absence or normal appearance.

Classification via prompt pairs.

For each prompt pair (pj−,pj+)(p_{j}^{{-}},p_{j}^{{+}}), we define a binary classifier based on cosine similarity in the shared embedding space:

hj(x)=𝕀[sim(fθ(x),pj+)>sim(fθ(x),pj−)],h_{j}(x)=\mathbb{I}\big[\text{sim}(f_{\theta}(x),p_{j}^{+})>\text{sim}(f_{\theta}(x),p_{j}^{{-}})\big], (2)

where sim​(x,p)\text{sim}(x,p) denotes the ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized cosine similarity.

3.2 Evolutionary prompt optimization

We formulate prompt discovery as a multi-objective optimization problem that balances classification accuracy, which measures the collective performance of hjj=1K{h_{j}}_{j=1}^{K} on the training set, with prompt diversity, which mitigates semantic redundancy by penalizing similar prompts in the text embedding space. To address this problem, we propose an evolutionary algorithm that operates directly within the VLM embedding space and uses LLMs to generate semantically grounded prompt mutations. An overview of the proposed framework is shown in Figure 1, and the components of the algorithm are described below.

Initialization.

We begin with a meta-prompt Q0Q_{0} that encodes key diagnostic observations, which is used to initialize the first-generation population:

P(0)={(pj−,pj+)}j=1K0,pj±∈𝒯,P^{(0)}=\{(p_{j}^{-},p_{j}^{+})\}_{j=1}^{K_{0}},\quad p_{j}^{\pm}\in\mathcal{T}, (3)

where pj+p_{j}^{+} specifies a disease-related observation and pj−p_{j}^{-} denotes its absence. The meta-prompt Q0Q_{0} template is as follows:

Give <K0K_{0}> distinct textual descriptions of pairs of visual discriminative features to identify <task description>. Only provide the output as Python code in the following format: prompts = list[tuple[negative: str, positive: str]].

Here, <<K0K_{0}>> is the desired population size and <task description> is instantiated for each task (e.g., ”melanoma in dermoscopy images”)

Fitness evaluation & population update.

Each prompt pair (pj+,pj-)(p_{j}^{\text{+}},p_{j}^{\text{-}}) is evaluated on the training set:

sj=ℳ⁡({hj​(xi),yi}xi,yi∈𝒟).s_{j}=\mathcal{M}\left(\left\{h_{j}(x_{i}),y_{i}\right\}_{x_{i},y_{i}\in\mathcal{D}}\right). (4)

where ℳ:{0,1}N×{0,1}N→ℝ\mathcal{M}:\{0,1\}^{N}\times\{0,1\}^{N}\to\mathbb{R} is a performance metric (e.g., accuracy, F1, or inverse binary cross-entropy).

Prompt pairs with sj≥αs_{j}\geq\alpha are retained in a memory buffer

𝒰(t)={(pj−,pj+,sj)∣sj≥α},\mathcal{U}^{(t)}=\{(p_{j}^{-},p_{j}^{+},s_{j})\mid s_{j}\geq\alpha\}, (5)

which aggregates high-performing prompts across generations. In practice 𝒰(t)\mathcal{U}^{(t)} is capped to maintain tractable diversity.

LLM-guided mutation.

Unlike traditional evolutionary operators, we employ an LLM to generate refined prompt variations. Given selected prompts and their performance feedback, the LLM is instructed, via meta-prompt QtQ_{t}, to create KtK_{t} new prompt pairs that: (1) capture distinct medical concepts, (2) yield better performance.

At each iteration, a subset of KsK_{s} prompt pairs is drawn from the memory buffer 𝒰(t)\mathcal{U}^{(t)} for mutation using roulette wheel selection [6] guided by fitness scores. This probabilistic strategy balances exploration of diverse prompts with a bias toward those of higher fitness. The structure of QtQ_{t} is shown below:

The task is to generate distinct textual descriptions pairs <task description>. Here are the best performing pairs in ascending order. High scores indicate higher quality.
Current Top <KsK_{s}> prompt pairs: <List of prompt pairs with normalized scores>
Write <KtK_{t}> new prompt pairs that are different from the old ones and have a score as high as possible. Formulate a strategy. Only provide the output as Python code...Let’s think step-by-step

The meta-prompt’s design is critical for effective generation. While sampled via roulette wheel for diversity, the in-context examples are framed as the ”top performing pairs” to provide a clear optimization signal. To counteract recency bias [20], these exemplars are sorted in ascending order of fitness. Based on findings from Yang et al. [20], scores are normalized to an integer range [60-90] for stability. Finally, Chain-of-Thought prompting [19] is enabled via ”Formulate a strategy” and ”Let’s think step-by-step” to elicit reasoned generation.

Crowding for Diversity.

After all TT generations have completed, we apply a crowding mechanism inspired by NSGA-II [2] to the final candidate pool 𝒰(T)\mathcal{U}^{(T)} to eliminate semantic redundancy. Candidate prompts are clustered by semantic similarity via an LLM guided by the meta-prompt QcrowdQ^{\text{crowd}}:

The task is to group textual description pairs...
<Numbered List of KcK_{c} prompt pairs>
Group the prompt pairs that has exactly same observation but differ only in language variations. Give the indexes of the grouped pairs in the output. Provide the output as follows: list[list[index:int]]. Make sure to include all pairs in the output, even if they are not grouped with others. Let’s think step by step

This prompt instructs the LLM to act as a semantic de-duplicator, grouping prompts that describe the same core observation despite linguistic differences. Within each cluster returned by the LLM, only the highest-scoring pair is retained. The resulting set of unique, high-performing prompts constitutes our final optimized prompt set, P∗P^{*}:

P∗←⋃c∈𝒞argmax(p−,p+,s)∈c​s.P^{*}\leftarrow\bigcup_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\underset{(p^{-},p^{+},s)\in c}{\textrm{argmax}}s. (6)

Final Prediction.

For the final prediction, the optimized set of prompts P∗⊆𝒰(T)P^{*}\subseteq\mathcal{U}^{(T)} is aggregated via weighted majority voting:

y^=𝕀[∑j=1K∗wjhj(x)>12∑j=1K∗wj],\hat{y}=\mathbb{I}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{K^{*}}w_{j}h_{j}(x)>\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{K^{*}}w_{j}\right], (7)

where each weight wjw_{j} is set to the corresponding fitness score sjs_{j} over validation data, ensuring that more reliable prompts contribute more strongly to the final decision.

The complete BiomedXPro framework is summarized in Algorithm 1.

4 Experiments and results

4.1 Experimental setup

We evaluate our proposed BiomedXPro framework on a diverse set of biomedical tasks, with a specific focus on its ability to generate interpretable and high-performing prompts for few-shot learning and generalization. All experiments were conducted using the same base models for a fair comparison and were run on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 Ti GPU.

Base models.

For the VLM, we employed BiomedCLIP [10] with a ViT-B/16 backbone, a model that has demonstrated state-of-the-art zero-shot classification on various biomedical benchmarks. For the LLM, we employed Gemma 3-27B-it [16], accessed via Google AI Studio with default model parameters (temperature, top-k, top-p).

Datasets.

We evaluate on three public benchmarks spanning diverse imaging modalities: Derm7pt [8] (dermoscopy), WBCAtt [17] (peripheral blood smears), and Camelyon17-WILDS [9] (histopathology). Camelyon17-WILDS enables domain generalization assessment, with hospitals serving as distinct domains, while Derm7pt and WBCAtt are used to evaluate interpretability and clinical relevance. Meta-prompts used for each dataset is provided in the supplementary material.

Experimental protocols and evaluation.

We consider three evaluation protocols. (i) Few-shot learning: varying the number of labeled samples per class (Nc∈1,2,4,8,16N_{c}\in{1,2,4,8,16}) to assess data efficiency. (ii) Clinical relevance: assessing whether high-fitness prompts capture clinically validated concepts, using Derm7pt and WBCAtt. For Derm7pt, we restrict to binary melanoma versus non-melanoma classification, while WBCAtt is extended to a multiclass setting via one-vs-rest binary classifiers. (iii) Domain generalization: training on three hospital domains of Camelyon17-WILDS and evaluating on the unseen hospital domain.

We compare against zero-shot BiomedCLIP and representative prompt-tuning approaches, including CoOp [24], CoCoOp [23], and their biomedical extensions BiomedCoOp [10] and XCoOp [1]. For all prompt-tuning baselines, we adopt the default hyperparameters (e.g., learning rate, training epochs, number of LLM prompts) from the official BiomedCoOp implementation to ensure a fair comparison. Given the class imbalance inherent in biomedical datasets, we use the F1-macro score as our primary evaluation metric. Given the class imbalance inherent in biomedical datasets, we use the F1-macro score as our primary evaluation metric.

BiomedXPro parameters.

The evolutionary search is run for 500 generations (T=500T=500), initialized with a population of 50 prompt pairs (K0=50K_{0}=50). In each generation, we sample 10 candidates (Ks=10K_{s}=10) for mutation and instruct the LLM to generate 10 new refinements (Kt=10K_{t}=10), while maintaining a memory buffer of up to 1000 pairs to preserve diversity. Fitness is evaluated using the inverse binary cross-entropy for the 1- and 2-shot settings, and the F1-macro score for higher-shot regimes. The fitness threshold α\alpha is set relative to the zero-shot baseline, ensuring that prompts performing below chance for the chosen metric are discarded. Final crowding is performed over 3 iterations on batches of 30 pairs. Results are averaged over three independent runs.

4.2 Results and analysis

Quantitative performance.

BiomedXPro consistently outperforms all baselines in the data-scarce few-shot regime (Table 1). Its advantage is most pronounced in the critical 1–8 shot range, demonstrating strong generalization across the diverse tasks and imaging modalities represented by the benchmarks.

A notable trend is the underperformance of BiomedCoOp, and XCoOp compared to standard CoOp and CoCoOp. We hypothesize that this stems from its reliance on a single static LLM-generated prompt to inject biomedical knowledge. In our optimization framework, we observed that single-query LLM prompts often yield suboptimal solutions, effectively constraining the search space and leading to weaker generalization. By contrast, BiomedXPro continually explores and refines prompt candidates, avoiding this limitation and converging toward a diverse ensemble of high-fitness solutions

Full-data regime.

To assess whether our method remains competitive in data-abundant settings, we evaluate on the full Derm7pt dataset. Results are shown in Table 2. BiomedXPro remains comparable to the strongest baseline (XCoOp), while offering the added advantage of interpretable prompts. This indicates that our framework does not sacrifice performance even when abundant labeled data is available.

Clinical relevance.

To validate that BiomedXPro learns clinically relevant concepts, we analyze the semantic alignment between the discovered prompts and the training data’s statistical features. Specifically, we compute the conditional probability P⁡(c​l​a​s​s∣o​b​s​e​r​v​a​t​i​o​n)P(class\mid observation) across the training dataset to ground our analysis. The full conditional probabilities are provided in the supplementary material. The following analysis demonstrates a strong correspondence between these statistics and the semantic content of the discovered prompts.

For the Derm7pt task, the analysis reveals a strong correlation. The most statistically significant indicator, ‘Linear Irregular’ vascular structures (P=0.80P=0.80), was captured by a high-fitness prompt pair (F1: 0.6523) contrasting a ’regular, linear arrangement’ with a ’chaotic, branching pattern.’ Other key features like the ‘Blue-Whitish Veil’ (P=0.59P=0.59) were also identified by high-scoring prompts (F1: 0.6667) that distinguished its absence from when it is ’present and associated with ulceration.’ Furthermore, the prompts with the highest F1-scores (up to 0.6741) corresponded to another strong indicator, ‘Atypical Pigment Network’ (P=0.55P=0.55), by providing nuanced descriptions such as ’variegated pigmentation with shades of brown, black, blue, and grey.’

Similarly, For Neutrophil classification on WBCAtt, the framework again captured the most predictive features. For instance, the presence of small granules (P=1.00P=1.00) was identified by a prompt contrasting ’clear and homogenous’ cytoplasm with cytoplasm that ”contains fine, pale lilac granules,” while the highly predictive unsegmented-band nucleus (P=0.85P=0.85) was described by a prompt distinguishing a ’predominantly spherical’ nucleus from one that is ”irregular and lobulated.” This consistent alignment across tasks demonstrates that the framework’s evolutionary process discovers and textually articulates statistically significant visual features in an interpretable manner. The complete prompt ensembles (P∗P^{*}) discovered for both Derm7pt and WBCAtt are provided in the supplementary material.

4.3 Ablation studies

Effect of prompt selection criteria.

We analyze the impact of the strategy for sampling mutation candidates by comparing our proposed Roulette Wheel Selection against two baselines: deterministic Best-N and uniform Random selection. As shown in Fig. 2, these baselines represent extremes of the exploration-exploitation trade-off. Best-N selection focuses purely on exploitation, leading to premature convergence in local optima, while Random selection’s pure exploration provides an inefficient and erratic search signal to the LLM. Our approach effectively balances this trade-off by probabilistically favoring higher-fitness candidates while maintaining sufficient randomness for exploration, resulting in the stable and consistent performance gains shown in the learning curves.

Impact of generation size per iteration.

We also analyze the number of prompt pairs generated per mutation step, comparing our choice of 10 against smaller (5) and larger (50) sets. As shown in Fig. 3, generating only 5 pairs leads to slow convergence, while a large set of 50 causes performance to plateau quickly after a strong start. While the precise reason for this degradation with a large generation size is unclear, this finding is consistent with prior work by Yang et al. [20], who also observed that a moderate number of generated instructions was optimal. Based on these findings, we utilize a generation size of 10, as it provides a favorable balance between refinement diversity and optimization stability while being more cost-effective in terms of token usage.

Effect of chain-of-thought prompting.

We investigated the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting by adding an instruction for the LLM to first ”formulate a strategy” and ”Let’s think step-by-step” for improvement before generating new candidates. As shown in Fig. 4, this addition leads to consistently better performance. Examples of CoT generated by the LLM are provided in the supplementary material.

Effect of initial population size.

We compare initial sizes K0K_{0} of 10, 30, and 50, and find that a larger initial population of 50 consistently outperforms the smaller sets (Fig. 5). This suggests that a broader initial semantic space provides a more robust foundation for the optimization, preventing premature convergence on a narrow range of concepts. We did not explore sizes beyond 50 due to the practical limitations of our LLM, which struggled to reliably generate a large and exact number of distinct prompts in a single query.

4.4 Limitations and future work

Dependencies on pre-trained models and data.

The efficacy of BiomedXPro is fundamentally dependent on two core components: the underlying LLM and VLM. The framework’s ability to generate clinically relevant prompts is inherently capped by the breadth and accuracy of the biomedical knowledge encoded within the LLM, creating a potential knowledge bottleneck. While state-of-the-art commercial models like GPT-4 (used by XCoOp [1] and BiomedCoOp [10]) contain extensive knowledge, their use in an iterative framework with hundreds of generations is prohibitively expensive, necessitating a trade-off between model capability and computational cost. Similarly, the framework’s performance is tied to the VLM’s ability to form a meaningful embedding space, and it may inherit biases from the VLM’s pre-training data, potentially affecting fairness across diverse patient populations, an important area for further investigation.

Architectural limitations and validation assumptions.

Architecturally, the proposed framework is formulated for binary classification. While effective in multiclass settings via a one-vs-rest scheme, this approach can lead to over-specialized negative prompts (pj−p_{j}^{-}) that describe a single competing class (e.g., contrasting ’Eosinophils’ with ’Neutrophils’) rather than a general negative case. Extending the framework to natively handle multiclass prompt sets (instead of a prompt pair) is a non-trivial future research direction that must address the combinatorial complexity of updating the prompt set. Another architectural limitation is that diversity is enforced via crowding only as a final post-processing step. We found that per-iteration LLM-driven clustering was unstable, sometimes erroneously grouping disparate prompts. Future work could integrate diversity maintenance at each optimization step by using a more deterministic semantic similarity metric on the prompts or the prompt embeddings. Furthermore, our validation approach in this work relies on training data statistics as a proxy for clinical importance, a measure that may itself be subject to dataset-specific biases.

Future work in clinical verification and grounding.

Finally, building full clinical trust requires deeper verification of the model’s reasoning. While our framework generates highly descriptive prompts (e.g., ’variegated pigmentation with shades of brown, black, blue, and grey’), future work is needed to verify that the VLM’s decision-making is truly sensitive to such nuanced details. A comprehensive validation would also require visual grounding analysis, using methods like Grad-CAM [15], to ensure the model’s spatial attention aligns with the features described in the prompts. Both steps, coupled with rigorous evaluation by clinical domain experts, are essential for ensuring the model’s reasoning process is robust and truly aligned with clinical practice.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we introduce BiomedXPro, an evolutionary framework that generates diverse ensembles of interpretable, natural-language prompts for biomedical image classification. Our method addresses the critical limitations of uninterpretable soft prompts and single-prompt systems by leveraging an LLM as both a biomedical knowledge extractor and an adaptive optimizer within an evolutionary search.

Our experiments demonstrate that BiomedXPro consistently outperforms state-of-the-art prompt-tuning methods in challenging few-shot and domain generalization settings across multiple biomedical datasets. Crucially, our analysis shows that the discovered prompts are not only high-performing but are also semantically aligned with statistically significant clinical features, grounding the model’s predictions in verifiable concepts. By directly addressing the fundamental needs for interpretability, diversity, and trustworthiness, BiomedXPro represents a significant step toward the safe and reliable deployment of advanced vision-language models in clinical practice.

Supplementary material

Meta-Prompts utilized for each dataset

This section presents the exact meta-prompts used for each dataset evaluated in this work.

Derm7pt [8] (Melanoma vs Non-melanoma binary classification)

  • •

    Q0Q_{0} — Initial meta-prompt

  • •

    QtQ_{t} — Mutation meta-prompt

  • •

    QcrowdQ_{\text{crowd}} — Crowding meta-prompt

WBCAtt [17] (Peripheral Blood Smears: Multiclass Cell-type classification)

The following meta-prompts were utilized for the WBCAtt dataset, which focuses on multiclass cell-type classification in peripheral blood smears. For each one-vs-rest binary classifier, the variables {BINARY_LABEL} and {other_labels_str} are replaced with the specific cell-type being evaluated. The prompt leverages a set of defining attributes for each white blood cell type, which are stored in the MEDICAL_CONCEPTS_MAPPING dictionary. These attributes are:

  • •

    Basophil: Nucleus=Segmented, NC Ratio=Low, Granularity=Yes, Color=Blue/Black (dense)

  • •

    Eosinophil: Nucleus=Segmented, NC Ratio=Low, Granularity=Yes, Color=Red

  • •

    Lymphocyte: Nucleus=Unsegmented, NC Ratio=High, Granularity=No, Size=Small

  • •

    Monocyte: Nucleus=Unsegmented, NC Ratio=Low, Granularity=No

  • •

    Neutrophil: Nucleus=Segmented, NC Ratio=Low, Granularity=Yes, Color=Blue

  • •

    Q0Q_{0} — Initial meta-prompt
